edition.basis: Revised 3rd edition (2004), 40 chapters; same chapter structure as the 2006 full-cast audiobook. 30th anniversary edition (2014) also has 40 chapters.
notes: 1st (1984) and 1986 editions: about 30 chapters (inferred); chapters 31-40 (division manager, five focusing steps, three questions) added by the 1992 2nd revised edition.
2004 3rd edition adds interviews (case studies) by David Whitford.
2014 30th anniversary edition: updated text, five focusing steps stated more explicitly, essay 'Standing on the Shoulders of Giants' (TOC and Toyota); interviews removed.
2006 audiobook: HighBridge Audio, full cast, about 11.5 h, from the 3rd edition.

Summaries disagree by one chapter for T/I/OE (6 vs 8), bottleneck discovery (18 vs 19), late-order priority (20 vs 21), Julie's if-then talk (38 vs 39). This file follows sum-fredlybrand-plot and sum-velocity.

chapters.title: One late order stops the plant
events_as_mechanism: One missing part holds a full customer order: the order is only as fast as its slowest part.
Expediting breaks setups on other work, so other orders slip.
Head office gives the plant 3 months before closure.

chapters.title: Expediting ships one order, delays others
events_as_mechanism: The late order ships only with overtime after a key machine (NCX-10) is repaired.
WIP is high everywhere, yet orders are late: busy is not productive.

chapters.title: Division numbers fail; measures do not guide
events_as_mechanism: Division-level reports show losses; the division has about one year.
Reported measures do not tell a plant manager what to do.

chapters.title: Robots raise efficiency, not profit
events_as_mechanism: A 36% efficiency gain in one area gives no increase in shipments and no cut in cost.
Jonah predicts high inventory and late orders from the efficiency claim alone.
jonah_questions: Did plant shipments go up after the robots?
Did inventory or headcount go down?
What is the goal of your company?

chapters.title: The goal is to make money
events_as_mechanism: Quality, cost, technology and jobs are tested one by one: each is a means, not the goal.
Full warehouses of unsold goods show that production is not sales.

chapters.title: Net profit, ROI and cash flow
events_as_mechanism: Three bottom-line measures define money-making for the whole firm.
They do not tell the floor what to do: an operational link is missing.

chapters.title: Decision to find Jonah
events_as_mechanism: Alex decides to fix the plant with a method, not with more expediting.

chapters.title: Throughput, inventory, operating expense defined
events_as_mechanism: Three operational measures replace local measures: money in (T), money held (I), money out (OE).
Throughput counts at the sale, not at production.
jonah_questions: What is the goal, in measures the floor can use?
Is a product in the warehouse throughput?

chapters.title: Robots judged by T, I, OE
events_as_mechanism: Robots run to keep their efficiency high and make parts no order needs.
Inventory goes up; throughput and OE stay flat.

chapters.title: Team adopts the measures
events_as_mechanism: Machines and buildings count as inventory (money held to sell later through depreciation).
Team checks every activity against the three measures.

chapters.title: Balanced plant goes bankrupt
events_as_mechanism: A plant that runs every resource efficiently builds excess stock.
Capacity cut to match demand at every resource gives missed shipments: fluctuations accumulate down a dependent chain.
jonah_questions: What happens when dependent events combine with statistical fluctuations?
Why is a plant with every capacity matched to demand close to bankruptcy?

chapters.title: Home conflict
events_as_mechanism: Personal goals conflict with job demands; the same goal question applies to life.

chapters.title: Scout hike: line spreads out
events_as_mechanism: The troop line spreads: gaps (inventory) grow behind slow walkers.
Troop arrival time equals the arrival time of the slowest walker.

chapters.title: Matchstick and dice game
events_as_mechanism: Five stations, each a die with average 3.5, pass matches in a line.
Output falls below 3.5 per round and queues grow: a station cannot use a high roll if no matches wait for it.

chapters.title: Herbie goes to the front
events_as_mechanism: Herbie at the front: the line cannot spread beyond his pace (release at constraint pace).
Other scouts carry Herbie's load: the constraint goes faster, so the troop goes faster.

chapters.title: Julie leaves
events_as_mechanism: No TOC mechanism; personal subplot.

chapters.title: Robot line test: fluctuations cap output
events_as_mechanism: A rush order of subassemblies depends on upstream rates that vary.
Robot capacity caps the line; a pile in front of it is what protects its output.

chapters.title: Find the bottlenecks
events_as_mechanism: Team compares demand hours with available hours per resource and looks at queues.
NCX-10 and heat treat have capacity below demand: these are the bottlenecks.
jonah_questions: Is a bottleneck good or bad?
Do you balance capacity or flow with demand?

chapters.title: Jonah tours the plant
events_as_mechanism: Bottlenecks stand idle at breaks and while waiting for parts.
Team values a lost bottleneck hour at about 2,735 dollars (plant OE / bottleneck hours); Jonah: it is the throughput of the whole plant.
Some parts go through heat treat with no need; bad parts get bottleneck time.
jonah_questions: Why is the bottleneck idle during lunch?
Must all these parts go through heat treat?
Can an old machine or a vendor do the same work?
Where is quality checked: before or after the bottleneck?

chapters.title: Plan to exploit the bottlenecks
events_as_mechanism: Team stages QC before bottlenecks, staggers breaks and runs late orders first on the bottleneck.

chapters.title: Red and green tags
events_as_mechanism: Red tags: parts for bottlenecks go first at every station; green: the rest.
About 90% of late orders wait for bottleneck parts.

chapters.title: First results; old machine back
events_as_mechanism: Late orders ship; average lateness falls.
An old machine returns to add capacity at the NCX-10 work.

chapters.title: Never starve the bottleneck
events_as_mechanism: Bottlenecks wait for workers between batches.
Dedicated crews and a foreman stay at each bottleneck.

chapters.title: Shortages appear in assembly
events_as_mechanism: Shipments set records, then final assembly lacks green parts.
The shortage looks like a new bottleneck.

chapters.title: Material released too fast
events_as_mechanism: Release by local efficiency piles red work in front of bottlenecks.
Non-bottlenecks spend time on red work too early, so green parts are late and assembly waits.
jonah_questions: Is the new shortage a new bottleneck or a release problem?
How do you release material only as the bottleneck needs it?

chapters.title: Drum and rope
events_as_mechanism: Material release is tied to the bottleneck schedule, as Herbie at the front.
Non-bottleneck workers can idle: idle time costs less than excess stock.

chapters.title: Plant must give 15% more
events_as_mechanism: The plant is the only profitable unit; the division asks for 15% more.
More throughput now needs more orders, not only more output.

chapters.title: Halve the batches
events_as_mechanism: Half batch size cuts queue and wait time, so lead time and WIP fall.
Extra setups at non-bottlenecks use idle time: no real cost.
jonah_questions: What if you cut batch sizes in half?
What does a setup at a non-bottleneck cost?

chapters.title: Small batches win an order
events_as_mechanism: Cost accounting shows a higher unit cost from more setups.
Short lead time in small weekly lots wins a large order.

chapters.title: Audit and inventory valuation
events_as_mechanism: Lower inventory reduces reported profit through valuation; the audit shows a smaller gain.
A large new customer order follows from short lead time.

chapters.title: Plant saved; Alex promoted
events_as_mechanism: The plant stays open on throughput results despite cost measures.
Alex becomes division manager: the system to manage gets larger.
jonah_questions: What must a manager do to run any system?

chapters.title: How Jonah taught
events_as_mechanism: Jonah asked; Alex found the answers, so he owned them and the team did too.

chapters.title: New division team
events_as_mechanism: The plant team takes division roles; the method must now work without Jonah.

chapters.title: What is a manager's job
events_as_mechanism: Team asks which process a manager uses on any system, not only a plant.

chapters.title: Periodic table: find the order
events_as_mechanism: Mendeleev's table shows that order in data lets you predict.
Team looks for the same order in its own steps.

chapters.title: Five focusing steps written
events_as_mechanism: Team writes the process it used: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat.
Throughput comes before cost cuts.

chapters.title: Inertia: old rules hold capacity
events_as_mechanism: Old release rules stay after the constraint moves and hold work back.
When removed, about 20% spare capacity appears: the constraint moves to the market.

chapters.title: Sell spare capacity in Europe
events_as_mechanism: A European order below normal price is taken: price is above variable cost and OE does not change.
Separate market, so domestic prices hold.

chapters.title: New bottlenecks, lead time grows
events_as_mechanism: More orders create new bottlenecks; lead time goes from 2 to 4 weeks and inventory rises.
Effect-cause-effect reasoning ('if this, then also that') finds the cause.

chapters.title: Three questions
events_as_mechanism: Alex and Lou trace the division problems to core causes.
Alex decides to be his own Jonah: what to change, to what to change, how to cause the change.
jonah_questions: What to change?
What to change to?
How to cause the change?
